name: Justin Niebank
sources: Mix — ACM Awards studio and industry winners (https://www.mixonline.com/news/acm-awards-studio-and-industry-winners-announced-2)
notes: The most-awarded mix engineer in country music. ⛔ **This file exists because the research says outright that it should**: "**Chuck Ainlay and Justin Niebank are placed in PRODUCERS** although they are primarily engineers/mixers, because their documented method (mic sets, chains, rough-mix-as-master, per-channel discipline) is exactly the kind of parameter set the app needs and **neither has an entry elsewhere**" (Assignment notes). The entry names the load-bearing parameter itself: "his philosophy is the load-bearing style parameter for the whole genre: **'I like to record performances; I don't like to record microphones.'** Model minimal corrective processing and maximum reliance on the take" — which is the loose quantize, the wide velocity spread and the real jitter here, and it is why nothing in this model is pushed toward a grid. The two moods are the entry's own per-song decision, quoted: "he documents two deliberately different kit setups. **Minimal (three mics): a Russian Oktava ribbon on kick, a Neumann U47 overhead, a Coles ribbon in the room.** **Full booth setup: AKG D112 kick, SM57 + AKG 451 snare top, SM81 snare bottom, Audio-Technica ATM-25s on toms, RØDE NT4 stereo overhead, Coles ribbon and RCA 44 room mics.** … So: choose between an intimate three-mic ribbon kit and a full close-miked kit as a per-song decision." ⚠ The translation from mic list to note content is INFERRED and it is one step: a kit with no tom mics does not play tom fills, so `three-mic ribbon kit` carries a cymbal-only perc set on a long fill grid with the wider dynamic range a room ribbon captures, and `full booth kit` — the only setup whose mic list names toms — carries the tom lanes on a short fill grid with the tighter, closer velocity band. The mic lists are researched; the numbers are not. The two weights are equal because the entry calls it a per-song decision and states no preference between them. ⚠ Authoring `modes` **replaces** the genre's radio/porch/riff-cut moods rather than adding to them, which is correct here: the documented choice on his sessions is which kit is up, not which radio format is being cut. The arrangement encodes the two working-method facts: "**'I like to have all of my options up on the board'** so the mix never stalls" and, most importantly, "**his rough mix of a No. 1 country single became the basis for the final master** — model the rough balance as the intended balance," so `switchUpProb` and the drop-out probability sit near the floor — the first balance is the intended one and the back half does not reinvent itself. ⚠ **No `session.bpm`, no `session.keys`, no `chords`, `melody` or `bassline` block.** The entry states "Keys: n/a," names no tempo and no numeral, and its Melody/chords line is a signal chain ("Waves amp modelling rather than re-amped; **TC Electronic M3000** for reverb") with no note content — so every one of those is inherited rather than invented. ⚠ Confidence is medium where the research says high: the mic lists, format chain and philosophy are all documented first-person, but almost none of it is note-level, so what a generator can act on here is thin.
